title: Clone Graph
pattern: graph traversal with a visited set / flood fill
statement:
A background job needs its own private copy of an undirected graph so that it can rewrite edges without disturbing the original. The graph arrives as an adjacency list `adj`, where `adj[i]` lists the neighbours of node `i`; the list is symmetric (`j` appears in `adj[i]` exactly when `i` appears in `adj[j]`) and may contain the same neighbour twice. Every id that appears in the lists, and `start` itself, is one of the nodes, so all of them lie in `0 .. adj.length - 1`. Copying is a traversal problem rather than an allocation problem: you start at the entry node `start`, walk the adjacency lists, and remember which nodes you have already copied so that a cycle does not send you round forever.

A grader cannot compare node identity, so report the structure you copied instead. Return every undirected edge inside the component that contains `start`, each written as `[u, v]` with `u <= v`; an edge is reported only when both of its endpoints sit inside that component. Every edge of the component appears exactly once, edges touching nodes outside the component are omitted, and the whole list is sorted ascending by first endpoint and then by second endpoint. When `start` has no neighbours, return an empty list.

The input never contains a self loop, so `adj[i]` never lists `i`.

Constraints: `1 <= adj.length <= 100`, `0 <= adj[i].length <= 99`, `0 <= adj[i][j] <= adj.length - 1`, `0 <= start <= adj.length - 1`.

constraints: Function signature: `function solve(adj: number[][], start: number)`.
Inputs are JSON-serializable values satisfying the bounds stated above.
hints: Cloning is a traversal: mark a node as copied the first time you meet it, before you look at its neighbours, or a cycle will revisit it forever.

Both approaches need the same reachable set; only the way the frontier is maintained differs. One rescans every list looking for newly reachable nodes, the other keeps the frontier in a stack or queue.
Once you have the reachable set, canonicalise each edge as (min, max), drop repeats with a set, and sort by the pair so the output is deterministic.

editorial.approach: The brute force is a flood fill without a frontier. It marks `start` reachable and then rescans the entire adjacency list over and over, promoting any node that neighbours a reachable one, stopping when a full pass discovers nothing new. That is a fixpoint computation: one wave costs O(V + E) and a long path-shaped component needs O(V) waves, so O(V * E). The optimal version replaces the repeated rescan with an explicit frontier: a stack (DFS) or queue (BFS) seeded with `start`, into which each node is pushed at the moment it is first discovered and marked, so every neighbour list is read exactly once, O(V + E). Either way the last step turns the reachable set into the required edge list: walk only reachable nodes, keep a neighbour only when it is itself reachable and inside `0 .. adj.length - 1`, canonicalise the pair as (min, max), de-duplicate through a hash set keyed on the pair, then sort.
editorial.why_optimal: Deciding whether a node belongs to the component requires looking at its adjacency list, so every node and every adjacency entry of the component must be touched at least once: O(V + E) is a lower bound and the frontier version attains it. The fixpoint version is a factor V slower because a node discovered late is only noticed when a later full pass sweeps past its predecessor. De-duplicating and sorting cost an extra O(E log E), which is dominated by the traversal.
editorial.pitfalls: For the traversal, forgetting to mark `start` before the loop (so a self-returning edge adds the component twice) and pushing a neighbour without marking it at push time, which lets a triangle re-push the same node and can loop forever on a cycle. Reading `adj[start]` while assuming `start` is one of the nodes: when `start` lies outside `0 .. adj.length - 1` the row does not exist, so the first step of the traversal has nothing to iterate and the run dies instead of reporting an empty component. Emitting an edge from a reachable node to a neighbour that is not itself reachable: such an edge leaves the component and must be dropped, which is exactly what the symmetric input makes easy to forget. For the output, emitting an edge twice because the input lists it from both endpoints, or twice from the same endpoint when a duplicate neighbour is present, instead of de-duplicating through a set. Building the key as `u + ',' + v` without normalising the order, so `0,10` and `10,0` never collapse and a phantom edge `[10, 0]` appears. Sorting with the default string comparison, which puts `[10, 2]` before `[2, 3]`.
